title: Minimum Absolute Difference in an Array
directAnswer: The closest two numbers in value are always adjacent once the array is sorted, so you never need to compare all pairs. Sort ascending, then scan consecutive pairs and return the smallest `|arr[i+1] − arr[i]|`. O(n log n) from the sort, O(n) for the scan.

remember.formula:
sort(arr)
best = ∞
for i in 1 .. n-1:
    best = min(best, arr[i] - arr[i-1])
return best
rules: After sorting, the minimum absolute difference is always between **adjacent** elements — no need to check distant pairs.
Once sorted, `arr[i] − arr[i-1]` is already non-negative, so you can drop the `abs()`.
Compare `n − 1` adjacent pairs, not all `n(n−1)/2` pairs — that's the whole point.
Handle negatives correctly: sorting orders by value, so `[-2, 2, 4]` gives gaps 4 and 2, not 0.
Use a wide type for the subtraction if values span the full int range — `−10⁹` to `10⁹` differences fit in int, but be deliberate.
whenToUse: Find the closest pair by value in a 1-D array
Minimise a gap and the array can be reordered freely
Any 'tightest pair / smallest spread' question on unstructured numbers
You can afford an O(n log n) sort
antiSignals: You must preserve original indices/positions and can't sort → different approach
Closest pair in 2-D / geometry → divide-and-conquer closest-pair, not this
You need the closest pair to a query value repeatedly → sort once then binary search
Difference defined on something other than value (e.g. index distance) → re-read
remember.takeaway: The closest two values are neighbours after sorting — a one-line fact that turns an O(n²) all-pairs scan into O(n log n). The same 'sort, then only adjacent matters' idea powers Max Min and many spread problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid the naive O(n²) all-pairs comparison by recognising that sorting makes the closest pair adjacent.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing every pair with a double loop, or forgetting to sort and then wrongly assuming adjacency in the original order.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Justify adjacency in one line: for any non-adjacent sorted pair (i, j), the elements between them are squeezed in value, so some adjacent pair has a difference no larger — checking neighbours suffices.

problemStatement:
Given an array of integers `arr`, find the **minimum absolute difference** between any two elements in the array.

The absolute difference of two elements `a` and `b` is `|a − b|`. Return the smallest such value over all pairs.
constraints: Elements may be negative and may repeat
There are at least two elements, so a pair always exists
understanding: We want the two numbers that are closest in value anywhere in the array. Positions don't matter — only how close two values are — so we're free to reorder. Duplicate values make the answer 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the pair have to be at adjacent indices in the original array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — any two elements anywhere. That freedom is exactly why we can sort.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain negative numbers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Sorting orders by signed value, so the adjacency argument still holds for negatives.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the minimum difference be 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, if any value repeats — two equal elements have difference 0, the smallest possible.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I return the difference or the pair itself?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the minimum difference. (If the pair is asked, track the index where the min occurs.)

examples.explanation: Sorted: [-7, 0, 3]. Adjacent gaps: 0−(−7)=7 and 3−0=3. Minimum is 3.
Sorted: [-3, 1, 17, 68, 71]. Adjacent gaps: 4, 16, 51, 3. Minimum is 3 (between 68 and 71).
Sorted, the closest neighbours are -54 and -53, a gap of 1.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Compare Every Pair
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to establish the baseline, then beat it by sorting.
hints: The minimum difference is over all pairs. What's the most direct way to consider every pair?
Two nested loops: for each i, for each j > i, track the smallest |arr[i] − arr[j]|.
This is correct but quadratic. Is there structure that lets you avoid most of these comparisons?
approaches.complexityReasoning: n(n−1)/2 pairs, each compared in O(1); no extra storage beyond a running minimum.
approaches.explanation:
Look at every unordered pair `(i, j)` with `j > i`, compute `|arr[i] − arr[j]|`, and keep the smallest seen.

**Why it's the natural first move.** The problem is defined over all pairs, so enumerating all pairs is the most faithful translation. It needs no insight and is trivially correct.

**Why `j` starts at `i + 1`.** Starting the inner loop above `i` visits each unordered pair once and never compares an element with itself (which would give a meaningless 0). It's the same loop hygiene as in Two Sum's brute force.

**Why we don't ship it.** With `n = 10⁵`, the pair count is ~5 billion — far too slow. The win comes from realising we don't need distant pairs at all: after sorting, the closest two values must be neighbours, so a single linear sweep replaces the nested loops.
approaches.insight: The quadratic scan wastes effort comparing far-apart values that can never be the closest pair. Sorting exposes the only comparisons that can matter — adjacent ones — collapsing n²/2 checks into n−1.

approaches.name: Sort + Adjacent Scan (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'sort, then the closest pair is adjacent'.
hints: If two numbers are close in value, where do they end up relative to each other once the array is sorted?
Sort ascending. The closest pair must be next to each other — otherwise a value squeezed between them would be even closer to one of them.
Scan i from 1 to n−1 and track the minimum of arr[i] − arr[i-1]. Since the array is sorted, that difference is already non-negative.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting costs O(n log n) and dominates; the single neighbour scan is O(n) with O(1) extra space (in-place sort aside).
approaches.explanation:
Sort `arr` ascending, then sweep once comparing each element with its immediate predecessor. The minimum of `arr[i] − arr[i-1]` over `i = 1 … n−1` is the answer.

**Why the closest pair is adjacent after sorting — the proof.** Sort the array so `arr[0] ≤ arr[1] ≤ … ≤ arr[n-1]`. Take any pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`. Their difference telescopes: `arr[j] − arr[i] = (arr[i+1] − arr[i]) + (arr[i+2] − arr[i+1]) + … + (arr[j] − arr[j-1])`. Every term on the right is a non-negative *adjacent* gap, and the whole sum is at least as large as any single term. So `arr[j] − arr[i]` is ≥ the smallest adjacent gap in that range. Therefore no non-adjacent pair can beat the best adjacent pair — checking neighbours is enough.

**Why we can drop the absolute value.** After sorting, `arr[i] ≥ arr[i-1]`, so `arr[i] − arr[i-1]` is already `≥ 0`. The `abs()` from the brute force becomes unnecessary — a small but telling simplification that shows you understand the invariant.

**Why negatives are no problem.** Sorting orders by signed value, so `[-7, 0, 3]` is already in the right order and the adjacency argument applies unchanged. The gap `0 − (−7) = 7` is computed correctly because subtraction respects sign.

**Why this is optimal in practice.** We do `n − 1` subtractions instead of `n(n−1)/2`. The only cost above linear is the sort, which is unavoidable in the comparison model for revealing adjacency. For `n = 10⁵` this is microseconds versus billions of operations.
approaches.insight: The telescoping argument is the heart of it: any gap is a sum of adjacent gaps, so the global minimum gap is a minimum over adjacent gaps. This 'distant differences decompose into adjacent ones' idea is why sorting helps so many spread/closeness problems — once sorted, locality of value equals locality of position.

edgeCases.behavior: Sorted [5,5]; adjacent gap 0 — duplicates give the minimum possible answer.
Sorted [-10,-10,0]; first gap is 0, which wins immediately.
Only one pair; gap 2·10⁹ — fits in a long if you compute it as long, or in int range arithmetic carefully.

pitfalls: Forgetting to sort and assuming adjacency in the original order.
Starting the scan at i = 0 — arr[i-1] is out of bounds.
Keeping abs() and then mishandling — harmless here but signals you missed that sorted gaps are non-negative.

commonMistakes: Comparing all pairs in O(n²) instead of sorting first.
Assuming the closest pair is adjacent in the ORIGINAL (unsorted) array.
Mishandling negatives by taking abs of values instead of differences.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the sort
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adjacency only implies closeness after sorting. Scanning neighbours of the raw array compares unrelated values and misses the true minimum.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Out-of-bounds on the first element
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Accessing arr[i-1] with i starting at 0 reads index -1. Start the scan at i = 1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(len(arr)):
    best = min(best, arr[i] - arr[i - 1])
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(1, len(arr)):
    best = min(best, arr[i] - arr[i - 1])

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Taking abs of the values, not the difference
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The metric is |a − b|, not ||a| − |b||. Abs-ing values first turns -3 and 3 into the same number and reports a false 0.

followupVariations.title: Max Min
followupVariations.hint: Generalise to picking k elements minimising max − min — slide a width-k window after sorting.

followupVariations.title: Minimum Absolute Difference (BST)
followupVariations.hint: Same idea on a BST: in-order traversal yields sorted values, then compare neighbours.

followupVariations.title: K Closest Elements
followupVariations.hint: Sort or binary search, then a width-k window around the target.

patternNote: Sort then adjacent scan. Recognise it for any 'closest pair by value' on a reorderable 1-D array — sorting makes the answer a neighbour comparison. Same backbone as Max Min (window size k) and Minimum Absolute Difference in a BST.
